title: The Transistor's Invention at Bell Labs (1947)
explainer: On December 16, 1947, Bell Labs physicists John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built the first working point-contact transistor - a solid-state device that could amplify and switch an electrical signal without the size, fragility, and heat of a vacuum tube. The device was publicly demonstrated at Bell Labs on December 23, 1947, and Bardeen, Brattain, and their supervisor William Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery. Every transistor packed onto the microcontroller chip you're wiring up here descends from that one germanium device switching current one contact at a time.

title: The Intel 4004 and the Birth of the Microprocessor (1971)
explainer: In 1971, a four-chip design that Intel engineers Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, and Stanley Mazor developed under contract for a Japanese calculator company became the 4004 - the first commercially available microprocessor, packing a complete programmable CPU with roughly 2,300 transistors onto a single chip. Before this, building a "computer" meant wiring together a cabinet of separate logic chips; the 4004 proved a general-purpose processor could instead be one piece of silicon, which is the exact idea that makes a microcontroller - a whole computer on a single chip - possible today.
